<description>
{
 "summary": "Omit the response body when answering HTTP HEAD requests in the internal HTTP server. While the response headers, including Content-Length, continue to reflect what a GET request would return per RFC 9110, the server no longer writes the payload bytes over the wire. Functional tests are added to verify raw socket responses for both RPC and REST endpoints.",
 "problem": "HTTP HEAD responses currently transmit the full response body along with headers. Because compliant HTTP/1.1 clients stop reading at the end of the header section for HEAD requests, the unread body bytes remain on keep-alive connections, corrupting subsequent responses when proxied through connection-pooling reverse proxies like nginx.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description documents RFC 9110 section 9.3.2 non-compliance and shows reproduction: 'JSONRPC server handles only POST requests' body is emitted with a 405 Method Not Allowed header on HEAD requests.",
  "PR description notes that because REST endpoints and the RPC 405 path answer HEAD without authentication, unauthenticated clients can trigger upstream keepalive connection desynchronization behind reverse proxies."

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.
